why: A kitchen-equipment maker with $230-365m revenue per product line, about 20% of $1.2-1.9bn markets, and 55-110 sales reps (roughly $2-5m revenue per rep) is believable.
Overseas market shares of 0.3-7.4% and profit margins of 12-38% for a hybrid seed breeder are believable.
Tourism funds credited with 0.3-0.9 percentage points of GDP growth per segment over ten years (about 3 points in all) in a large country with $850bn GDP is believable.
An online training firm with twelve courses earning $2-46m each (about $170m in all) and 4-51 trainers per course is believable.
An online pet store with first-year profit of $0.5-22 per customer against 90-day revenue of $68-377 and $52-68 per order reflects thin but believable retail margins.
Bottled water consumption of about 117-140 litres per person a year, with bottle prices of $0.4-1.0 and costs of $0.1-0.4, is believable.
A seed company with about 20% of $1-2.4bn seed markets and 50-65 reps per crop is believable, even if maize revenue of about $8m per rep is high.
Payroll software spending of $56-392m per customer segment in an unnamed market, with modest past growth and faster forecast growth, is believable.
A gym chain surveying 13,000 recent members and 26,000 non-members, with each rating distribution summing to 100%, is believable.
A pet food market of about $45bn split into $22.6bn dry, $18.7bn wet and $4.1bn fresh, with fresh forecast to more than double in five years, is believable.
